say.text: Start with the exam. A stem asks for the **most common** gallstone type, as the previous-year (PYQ) key expects. Predict the key's answer.

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which source the question follows: the old exam key, or the current textbook grouping.
Yes. The exam key gives mixed stones as the most common type.
Texts group cholesterol and mixed stones together as the majority, about 80 per cent. Know both: the key for the exam, the grouping for practice.
That is not right.
It tempts you because Western texts rank cholesterol stones highest, but this stem asks for the exam key's answer.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check which source the question follows. The key and the text do not always agree here.

say.text: That is not right.

Current texts put cholesterol and mixed stones together as the large majority, so both answers are defensible in practice.
A boy with hereditary spherocytosis has chronic haemolysis for years. Predict his gallstone: which type, and where does it form?

choices.label: Black pigment stones, in the gallbladder
Brown pigment stones, in the bile ducts
Black pigment stones, in the bile ducts
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Follow the bilirubin. What does constant red cell breakdown push into the bile?
Yes. Chronic haemolysis gives black pigment stones, which form in the gallbladder.
They are small, multiple and hard, and they go with cirrhosis too.
That is not right.
It tempts you because it names the bile ducts, but you have tied the site to infection rather than to the cause in this boy.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pair each colour with its cause first, then with its site.

say.text: That is not right.

say.text: Haemolysis gives black pigment stones: small, multiple and hard, formed in the gallbladder, and linked with cirrhosis.
Brown pigment stones are different: soft and earthy, in the bile ducts, with infection and stasis.
A man with recurrent cholangitis and an Ascaris infestation has soft, earthy stones in his bile ducts. Predict the stone type and what drives it.

choices.label: Brown pigment stones, from bacterial infection in the ducts
Black pigment stones, from haemolysis in the gallbladder
Black pigment stones, from haemolysis in the bile ducts
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the bacteria in infected bile do to bilirubin, and where the stone then forms.
Yes. Infected bile carries bacterial β-glucuronidase, which frees bilirubin to form soft brown stones in the ducts.
Ascaris and Clonorchis are the parasites linked to them.
That is not right.
It tempts you because haemolysis is in the picture, but this stone is a duct problem driven by infection, not by red cell breakdown.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask what the stem gives as the cause before you pick the colour.

say.text: That is not right.

say.text: Biliary infection brings bacterial β-glucuronidase, which frees bilirubin from its conjugates.
The free bilirubin forms soft, earthy brown stones in the bile ducts, linked with parasites such as Ascaris and Clonorchis.
Female, fat, fertile, forty: the mnemonic for cholesterol stones.
Oestrogen raises biliary cholesterol and progesterone slows the gallbladder, so pregnancy and the pill both raise risk. Rapid weight loss, including after bariatric surgery, does too.
Compare acalculous with calculous cholecystitis. Predict how acalculous disease behaves.

choices.label: Has more gangrene and perforation, and higher mortality
Runs a milder course, since no stone blocks the duct
Has lower mortality, since patients are younger
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what drives the inflammation when no stone is present, and in whom it occurs.
Yes. Without a stone, the gallbladder is inflamed by stasis and ischaemia, so gangrene and perforation are more frequent.
Its mortality is higher as well.
That is not right.
It tempts you because no stone means nothing blocks the duct, so the course looks gentler. The question is what drives the inflammation.

sure_note.text: You were sure that no stone means milder. Check what drives inflammation in acalculous disease.

say.text: That is not right.
It tempts you because the group sounds benign, but severity follows the illness the patient is in, not the patient's age.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so link the severity to the setting in which acalculous disease arises.

say.text: Acalculous cholecystitis is inflammation with no stone, in about 5 to 10 per cent of cases.
It arises from stasis and ischaemia in critically ill patients after surgery, trauma, burns, sepsis or prolonged fasting. It carries more gangrene, perforation and higher mortality.
A patient with extensive burns on day 6 in the ICU develops fever and right upper quadrant tenderness. No stone is seen. What is the main risk to plan around?

choices.label: High risk of gangrene and perforation in this patient
Mild disease that can be watched without imaging
Settles with analgesia, as in biliary colic
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what is happening to the gallbladder wall in a sick patient, not whether a stone is there.
Yes. Stasis and ischaemia in a critically ill patient drive gangrene and perforation, so the risk is high.
That is not right.
It tempts you because nothing is blocking the duct, but this gallbladder is failing from stasis and ischaemia.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask what is injuring the wall before you judge how mild it is.

say.text: That is not right.
It tempts you because pain that settles is the colic pattern, but fever and tenderness point to inflammation of the gallbladder.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check whether the stem describes a passing colic or an inflamed gallbladder.

say.text: Fever and tenderness in this burns patient mean inflammation of the gallbladder, with no stone to explain it.
Stasis and ischaemia in critical illness progress to gangrene and perforation, so the risk is high and mortality is higher.
